title: Awe walks
hook: in a study, older adults who took weekly "awe walks" reported more joy (Sturm et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heschel's radical amazement at the ordinary. Your line was fearfully and wonderfully made. Last week belonged to scholars and naturalists. This week, the lab steps in.

Arm out, phone up, a quick selfie at the start of a walk. Again halfway. Again at the end. Week after week, a group of older adults did exactly this for a research team. The walks were short. Nobody climbed anything. When the researchers later laid the photos side by side, something had shifted in one group's pictures. The people in them took up less of the frame, and their smiles had changed. That group had been given one small extra instruction before they set out.
screen: `A SELFIE AT THE START.` → `WEEK AFTER WEEK.` → `SOMETHING SHIFTED IN THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: The study comes from Virginia Sturm and her colleagues. First, the setup. Everyone walked. One group just walked. The other was asked to take an awe walk: to go with fresh eyes, as if seeing things for the first time, and to notice what was vast and what was small. A cloud bank, a stretch of sky, the pattern on a leaf. Same legs, same shoes; only the attention changed. Second, what the awe walkers reported. More awe, as you'd expect, but also more joy and more of the warm, outward feelings like gratitude and compassion, gains the researchers reported growing over the weeks. Third, the photos. In the awe group, people took up less of their own selfies as time went on: more sky, more trees, a little less self. Researchers call this the small self, the sense that you're one part of something larger. And the smiles grew stronger. Smaller, and happier, at the same time. Fourth, a walker from long before would have recognized this. Henry David Thoreau wrote an essay simply called Walking. He opens with the word saunter, and offers two playful stories of where it came from: wanderers heading to the Holy Land, or people with no particular home, at home everywhere. For Thoreau, even the shortest walk could be taken in a spirit of adventure. The study and the essayist land in the same place: you don't need a mountain, just a different kind of looking, on the block you already know.
screen: `SAME WALK, DIFFERENT ATTENTION.` · `MORE JOY, MORE GRATITUDE.` · `A SMALLER SELF IN THE FRAME.` · `THOREAU'S SAUNTER.` · then, large: `SMALLER, AND HAPPIER.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly around the room or out a door, or, if you can't, let your eyes do the walking out the nearest window, with the awe walk's one instruction: fresh eyes. Find one thing that is vast, a sky, a ceiling, a long view, then one thing that is tiny, a crack, a thread, a leaf. Go back and forth between them, and let yourself be small for a minute.
Awe walks. Ordinary walks taken with fresh eyes, noticing the vast and the small. In one study, the walkers reported more joy. Today's word.
Your line: awe walk. Same route, fresh eyes, a smaller self in the frame. Day one thousand thirty, done.

howItsDone: People who take awe walks go on ordinary walks with the intention of noticing vast and tiny things with fresh eyes; some walk the same route regularly, and some take a photo along the way.

notes: Editor: rewrote the garbled hook lines about the faces in the frame; 'an older walker' (ambiguous beside the study's older adults) changed to 'a walker from long before'.

Study details to confirm against the paper: participants were older adults; the awe group was instructed to approach walks with fresh eyes and notice vast and small details; awe walkers reported more awe, joy and prosocial positive emotions (gratitude, compassion), with gains reported as growing over the weeks; selfies showed participants taking up less of the frame over time and more intense smiles. The voice gives no sample size, duration or effect sizes.
'Researchers call this the small self' — confirm the term is the study's.

Thoreau's 'saunter' derivation (à la Sainte Terre) is fanciful; the script calls both of Thoreau's derivations (à la Sainte Terre; sans terre, at home everywhere) 'playful stories' — confirm that framing.

Auditor: review no longer calls last week's figures poets and philosophers; Thoreau no longer said to have 'loved' saunter, and 'a small pilgrimage' replaced with his own framing (the shortest walk taken in a spirit of adventure).
The index hook carries a year (2020); dropped from the voice and hook line under the claims rule; the source ref keeps the citation.
